title: 9041 Data Viz ‘Bird Sightings at Sea (1969-1990)’
text:
Scientific Article Version A

Introduction
Historical observations are vital for future work in the field of conservation and biodiversity for scientists to better understand how the natural world changes in the wake of human influence. In ship logs from Captain John Jekins, estimated numbers of bird observations (flocks) and various behaviors alongside human activities aboard ships are recorded. This work shows the avian and human interactions observed over 21 years (1969-1990). I hypothesize that bird behavior will be influenced by ship activity. I also hypothesize that season will show a significant difference in bird behavior.


Methods
Data was taken from the tidytuesday weekly dataset collection on GitHub uploaded 2026-04-14. Dataframes birds and ships are combined for analysis. Overall there are 49019 observations recorded from this dataset. The dataset is extended to allow for each unique recorded behavior to be listed in a new column so as not to lose data from observations with birds observed doing more than one behavior. Lowest recorded ship activities and bird behaviors were removed from the dataset. Ship activity and bird behavior were tested together using a ChiSquare Test to determine significance. Graphs were made to show the average behaviors recorded across different seasons and the average estimated number of flocks observed participating in certain behaviors across the seasons.





  



Figure 1












Figure 2













Figure 3













Figure 4







Results
In this data set, we see that bird behavior is observed to have some correlation with ship activity (ChiSquare Test), though the test is most likely skewed due to the low number of recorded observations during different ship activities. One can see frequency of ship activities greatly leans towards steaming and sailing Figure 1. In Figure 1 Figure 2we can see that most of the observations of bird behavior was seen while the ship was sailing, where a majority of behaviors were the birds seen following or flying past the ships. In the two categories with less observations we see less birds following the ship and more accompanying or flying past. We can also see the birds are seen feeding as well during line fishing and trawling.  In Figure 2  @fig-ggfig2 we see a peak in overall observations of birds flying past in the summer and steep decline in the winter, while in the spring there’s more following the ship in the spring and less in the autumn. In Figure 3 Figure 4 we see a peak in the numbers of birds of naturally feeding and feeding in the spring. We also see a decline in numbers of birds observed in the winter and autumn in general.


Conclusion
From this dataset we can see fluctuations in avian behavior across the seasons and during activities on a ship with a trend of feeding increase during the spring and summer and a general observation of birds accompanying ships while fishing. It would be interesting to see more observations of avian behavior around fishing boats from the past and now present.

title: 9041 Data Viz ‘Bird Sightings at Sea (1969-1990)’
text:
Version B: Accessible/Dynamic Outlet

New Zealand Bird Sightings Across the Sea
While out at sea, Captain John Arthur Francis Jenkins would keep a log of the birds his crew would observe on his travels across the Pacific Ocean, from the Tasman Sea to the Southern Ocean of Antarctica. During his travels spanning 21 years (1996-1990) he would record the number of birds, their names, age, sex, plumage phases, and behaviors alongside a record of the weather, season, location, and activities on the ship. All of these records are kept at The Museum of New Zealand in Te Papa Tongarewa, of which we can observe through the help of GitHub’s tidytuesday dataset collection! With the danger of bird population decline, these observations can give us a glimpse into the past of what once was with abundance of bird populations. Let’s take a look. We will investigate how many and what kinds of birds are observed during different activities on the ship. What behaviors do these birds have at different activities?








Figure 5













Figure 6







Southern Ocean bird behavior and ship activity
We see that birds were often seen while the ship was sailing and still on the sea waters. During the times the crew would be fishing we can uncover a little more about what the captain would see when watching the birds. Often times the birds would follow or just fly past the ship while they were sailing. But while the crew was fishing, more birds would stay with the ship and we also see more of them feeding. In this context, feeding means they were most likely feeding on the fish the crew was working on catching. Interestingly they hardly would see the birds naturally feeding. When the ship was still however, we can see an even amount of seen behaviors where they’re feeding, flying past, accompanying the ship, and swimming in the water. Figure 5


Seasonal bird behaviors
Each time they would see a species of bird they’d estimate how many they saw, sometimes a few and other times thousands! Over the years, with thousands of birds seen, they were able to track a pattern in the how many birds were present on their journey and with that they also were able to track how the most frequent bird behaviors in the Southern Ocean across the seasons. In the spring a spike of birds would be seen, with an average of 1500 birds naturally feeding along with around 600 birds feeding with the crew, most likely while they drew in the ample fish swimming through the seas. The birds were seen less thereafter with the least seen in the fall. Figure 6


Closing statement
Long term datasets hold a wealth of knowledge for all interested in the unknown and these logs are no different. We can take records like this and compare it to what we see today. Do we see the same number of birds flying by ships today? Are more birds feeding on food from ships than before? Have their behaviors shifted across the seasons because of climate change? So many questions which can lead to so many solutions.

title: Data Viz
text:
The goal of this assignment is not simply to make several good-looking graphs. Your goal is to use a sequence of visualizations to communicate an empirical story: to guide a reader through a question, pattern, comparison, complication, or resolution in a deliberate order.
A useful test: if your figures could be rearranged in any order without changing the meaning of the presentation, you probably have a collection of plots rather than a data story.
You will then tell the same underlying story twice. The evidence should remain the same, but your design choices, level of technical detail, prose, annotations, and use of interactivity should reflect two different communication settings:

A scientific article
An accessible/dynamic web-based outlet

At least two substantive data visualizations are required in each version.




By completing this assignment, you should be able to:

Identify a clear empirical message in a dataset and organize evidence into a coherent narrative arc.
Create multiple visualizations that perform distinct jobs within that narrative rather than redundantly displaying the same result.
Use R to produce polished, reproducible data visualizations and a rendered web document.
Adapt visualization design and explanatory text to different audiences and publication contexts.
Distinguish scientific precision and technical reporting from public-facing clarity, accessibility, and engagement.
Use Git and GitHub to make the complete analysis reproducible and GitHub Pages to publish the finished work.

title: Data Viz
text:
Version A: Scientific Article
Present your story as though the figures and accompanying text were being prepared for a conventional scientific journal article.
Prioritize precision, interpretability, reproducibility, and technical completeness.
Your scientific version should generally:

Use static figures.
Be fully interpretable in black-and-white or greyscale as is often required by scientific journals. Do not rely on colour to encode essential information.
Use conventional scientific labels, units, scales, legends/direct labels, and figure captions as appropriate.
Report technical information needed to interpret the visualization—for example, sample sizes, uncertainty, model quantities, or definitions where relevant.
Keep decorative elements restrained. The visual hierarchy should emphasize the data and the scientific point.
Use prose appropriate for a scientifically literate reader. Technical terminology is appropriate when it improves precision.

title: Data Viz
text:
Version B: Accessible / Dynamic Outlet
Now present the same empirical story for an audience encountering it through an engaging web article, explainer, or similar public-facing medium.
Prioritize clarity, accessibility, narrative flow, and reader engagement without changing or overstating the evidence.
Your accessible/dynamic version might:

Use plain-language, takeaway-oriented headings and explanatory text.
Use colour, highlighting, direct annotation, icons, small multiples, or other design devices when they help guide attention.
Use interactive or dynamic elements—for example, tooltips, filters, animation, or plotly—when they add genuine explanatory value. Interactivity is cool, but is not required for its own sake.
Reduce unnecessary technical detail in the main visual display while preserving enough context for the claims to be understood accurately.
Make deliberate accessibility choices: readable text, sufficient contrast, sensible colour use, clear labels, and alternatives to colour-only encoding.
Think about pacing. Guide the reader through the evidence rather than confronting them with all available information at once.


Important: Adaptation Is Not Decoration
The two versions should not simply be identical figures with a different ggplot2 theme applied.
Your choices should demonstrate that you understand how audience and medium change what information is foregrounded, how it is explained, and how the reader’s attention is directed, while the underlying empirical claims remain consistent.

title: Data Viz
section: 1. Good Authority: Republicans’ Fascination with Testosterone, in Three Charts
text:
1. Good Authority: Republicans’ Fascination with Testosterone, in Three Charts
https://goodauthority.org/news/republicans-fascination-with-testosterone-in-three-charts/
This is close to the scope of the story expected for this assignment.
Pay particular attention to how three relatively conventional plots become an argument through sequencing. Each visualization answers or develops something raised by the previous one, while the prose explains why the next piece of evidence matters.
Notice that the effectiveness of the piece does not depend on technically elaborate visualizations. The strength comes from deciding:
What should the reader see first? What question does that create? What evidence should they see next?

title: Data Viz
text:
2. The Economist: The Banana Index
Data and materials:
https://github.com/TheEconomist/banana-index-data
This example illustrates how repeating a visual grammar while changing the analytical perspective can itself tell a story.
The comparison changes depending on how the environmental impact of food is evaluated—for example, relative to weight, calories, or protein.
Pay attention to how holding much of the visual form constant makes it easier for the reader to focus on the thing that is changing: the basis of comparison.
This is also an excellent example of making a potentially technical measurement issue intuitive and visually accessible.

title: Data Viz
section: 3. The Pudding: Is the Love Song Dying?

title: Data Viz
text:
Learning from the Exemplars
Do not imitate these examples mechanically.
Instead, use them to study how authors decide:
What does the reader see first?
What question or tension does that create?
What evidence comes next?
How does that evidence change what the reader thinks about the previous visualization?
What should the reader conclude by the end?
That sequence—not simply the number or attractiveness of the plots—is what turns several visualizations into a data story.
